title: Newbold's shorthand claims are not auditable as a key: his own editor reports seeing 8 strokes where Newbold saw 25, and the final step of the method chooses Latin by sense
statement: I read the open scan of William Romaine Newbold, The Cipher of Roger Bacon, ed. Roland Grubb Kent (1928), https://oncle-dom.fr/biblio/1928-Newbold-The%20Cipher%20of%20Roger%20Bacon.pdf, foreword pp. xiv-xix and the method chapters, and traced the six stages the step names. The verdict is that no runnable key can be built, and the reason is not effort but two properties of the method itself. (1) Stage one requires a transcription of microscopic shorthand marks that do not exist in EVA or v101 input. The marks are inside the ink strokes, often superimposed, sometimes covered by a blot or crossed by a line drawn to make several characters read as one heavy stroke (pp. xiv-xv). This is a measurement problem on the scan, not a parsing problem on the text, and it has no ground truth: the quantity to be measured was produced by the claimant, not by the manuscript. (2) The last stage produces a meaningless string over an eleven-letter alphabet and then REARRANGES it into Latin by choosing words that fit the sense. Kent states the difficulty plainly: 'The possibilities of such rearrangement seem too many for any certainty in the results'. A rule that picks the Latin by whether it makes sense cannot be frozen into a key, because the key's output is the input to a choice no deterministic program can make. The decisive negative evidence is in Kent's own foreword and is independent of our test: when he looked through Newbold's microscope and copied the tiny strokes himself, 'where I had seen eight strokes at most, he had seen twenty-five'. Kent also records that Newbold 'often examined a group of characters for two hours before he started to draw what he had seen', and that he restricted his time on the manuscript 'on account of the eyestrain involved'. So the mark inventory was never reproducible even between the two people closest to the work, which is exactly the agreement test the step asks for, and it failed a century ago. Newbold himself conceded the method's limits: he told Kent he had tried it on Bacon works obviously not in cipher and, while he could form Latin words for a time, he was 'soon left with unmanageable groups of consonants'. That is a self-report that the method manufactures Latin out of non-Latin input, which is the failure mode our kill tests are built to catch. The step's own remedy is therefore correct and is the whole answer: fix magnification and a mark inventory, transcribe blind, and measure agreement including repeat annotation of the same crop. Until that exists there is nothing to run through the judge, and under our rules a claim with no key is not a result, whatever its historical importance.
check: No attack.json is filed, because there is no key to attack: filing one would require inventing the mark transcription, which would be our claim and not Newbold's. The auditable step, if anyone takes it, is the one the step already states: fix plate or canvas coordinates, a magnification and a closed mark inventory before any annotation; have independent annotators transcribe public samples without being shown the proposed Latin; measure agreement on mark identity and on mark order, including repeated annotation of the same crop by the same annotator. Only if that agreement is high is there a transcription to freeze, after which the pair conversion and a deterministic recomposition rule can be stated and the resulting Latin scored against matched shuffled inputs. The recomposition rule is where the proposal is most likely to fail, since the historical method resolves the final ambiguity by sense.

evidence.source: W. R. Newbold, The Cipher of Roger Bacon, ed. R. G. Kent (1928), open scan; foreword pp. xiv-xix, chapters VI-IX
evidence.kent_sees_8_strokes_where_newbold_saw_25: foreword, p. xviii: 'where I had seen eight strokes at most, he had seen twenty-five'
evidence.eyestrain_limit: foreword, p. xviii, progress report to Provost Penniman, 14 Dec 1913
evidence.self_report_on_non_cipher_texts: foreword, p. xvii: formed Latin for a time, then 'unmanageable groups of consonants'
evidence.stages: six stages, foreword p. xvi: identify and transcribe marks in order; double all but first and last; divide into pairs; commute letters next to conmuta or q; translate pairs to alphabetic then phonetic values; rearrange into Latin
evidence.marks_absent_from_input: the marks are inside strokes and not represented in EVA or v101
evidence.verdict: not auditable as a key; the agreement test the step proposes already failed between Newbold and Kent
